processing: Its method is not documented. The name means square tea of Shizhou, which suggests a pressed shape, as was common for Tang tea, but that is an inference from the name.
appearance_dry: Not documented; the name suggests square pieces.
appearance_liquor: Not documented; no reliable description of the historical liquor exists.
taste_profile: No description of its taste survives in accessible records. Any tasting note attached to this name today describes a modern product and not the historical tea.

brewing.notes: No historical method applies. These are general starting numbers for a modern green tea, in case a modern tea carrying this name turns up.

vintage_note: Not on the market as a recognised tea with seasons or vintages; it survives as a name in lists of Hubei's Tang-period teas. If a shop offers it, treat it as a modern revival and ask what it actually is.
description:
Shizhou Fang Cha is a historical name more than a tea you can buy. It appears among the teas credited to Hubei in the Tang period, alongside names such as Qimen Tuanhuang and Xianrenzhang. Shizhou is the old name for the Enshi area in the southwest of the province.

The name is nearly all there is to go on. Fang means square, which hints at pressed pieces, and pressed tea was normal in the Tang. How it was actually made is not recorded in anything accessible.

It is listed here as green tea only because that is the nearest modern class; Tang tea did not fit today's categories neatly. Do not trust a confident tasting note for it.

If you want to taste the region today, look at modern Enshi green teas such as Enshi Yulu, while keeping in mind that they are separate teas and not descendants of this one, as far as anyone can show.
history: Hubei tea histories list Shizhou Fang Cha among the province's Tang-dynasty products. Little else is documented: no maker, no method and no account of when the name dropped out of use.
